t.5.44.1: Learning that the sons of his ministers had been slain by the great-souled monkey, Rāvaṇa, concealing his feelings, formed an excellent resolve.
t.5.44.3: Daśagrīva commanded the heroes, skilled in strategy, who were eager to capture Hanūmān and equal to the wind in speed in battle.
t.5.44.2: He commanded Virūpākṣa and Yūpākṣa, the rākṣasa Durdhara, Praghasa and Bhāsakarṇa, the five foremost leaders of the army.
t.5.44.4: "Go, all of you, leaders at the head of the army, backed by a mighty force, together with horses, chariots and elephants, and let that monkey be punished!"
t.5.44.5: Whatever may indeed befall them on encountering that forest-dweller, the task must still be accomplished, set against the demands of place and time.
t.5.44.6: Judging by his deeds, I do not think him a mere monkey. In every way it is a mighty being, possessed of great strength, or perhaps it was created by Indra through the power of his austerities on our account.
t.5.44.7: The Devas, Asuras and great Ṛṣis, together with the Nāgas, Yakṣas and Gandharvas, have been vanquished by all of you united together with me.
t.5.44.9: And this monkey of fierce prowess must not be underestimated by you, for I have seen monkeys that are swift and of vast valour.
t.5.44.8: Surely some wrong must be done to us by them; this is that very thing, there is no doubt about it. Let it be seized by force.
t.5.44.10: Vālin together with Sugrīva, and Jāmbavant of great strength, and Nīla, the commander of the army, and the others, Dvivida and the rest.
t.5.44.12: This must be understood as a mighty being that has taken on the form of a monkey. Exerting great effort, let him be subdued.
t.5.44.11: Yet theirs was no such fearsome speed, nor such fiery energy, nor such valor; nor such intelligence, nor such strength and zeal, nor such power of assuming forms.
t.5.44.14: Even so, one who knows the right course of conduct and desires victory in battle must protect himself with diligence, for success in war is fickle.
t.5.44.13: Indeed, the three worlds together with Indra, with the Suras, Asuras and men, are not able to stand before you on the field of battle.
t.5.44.15: All of them, of great might, having accepted their master's command, sprang up with tremendous speed, blazing with a splendour equal to that of fire.
t.5.44.17: Then the heroes beheld that great monkey, blazing like the rising sun, garlanded with the rays of his own splendour.
t.5.44.16: They were well furnished with chariots and with rutting elephants, with horses of great speed, with sharp weapons of many kinds, and with all their forces.
t.5.44.19: The moment they saw him, all of them, stationed in every direction, rushed at him from all sides with their various fearsome weapons.
t.5.44.18: Him who stood upon the archway, of great speed and great courage, of great strength and great wisdom, of great zeal, of mighty body and mighty power.
t.5.44.21: Pierced in the head by those five arrows, the monkey leapt up into the sky, roaring and making the ten directions resound.
t.5.44.20: Durdhara loosed upon his head five sharp, gleaming iron arrows with yellow tips, which looked like the petals of a lotus.
t.5.44.22: Then the heroic and mighty Durdhara, mounted on his chariot with his bow strung and ready, rushed forward, scattering many hundreds of arrows.
t.5.44.23: That monkey held him back in the sky as he rained down arrows, just as the wind at the close of the rainy season drives back a rain-laden cloud.
t.5.44.24: Then, tormented by that Durdhara, the son of the Wind roared once more, and, full of impetuous force, he grew larger.
t.5.44.25: Springing suddenly far up into the air, that monkey of great speed fell upon the chariot of Durdhara, like a mass of lightning falling upon a mountain.
t.5.44.26: Then Durdhara, abandoning that chariot whose eight horses had been crushed and whose axle and pole were shattered, fell to the ground, his life gone.
t.5.44.28: The mighty-armed monkey, having swiftly leapt up and stationed himself in the clear sky, was struck on the chest by those two with their two maces.
t.5.44.27: Seeing him fallen upon the ground, Virūpākṣa and Yūpākṣa, the invincible subduers of foes, sprang up, their fury roused.
t.5.44.29: Having struck down the onrush of those two swift ones, the mighty one, whose valour equalled that of Suparṇa, descended once more to the ground.
t.5.44.30: That monkey, the son of the Wind, reached a sāla tree and uprooted it, and with it he slew both those heroic rākṣasas.
t.5.44.33: Praghasa struck the best of monkeys with a sharp-pointed paṭṭiśa, and the rākṣasa Bhāsakarṇa struck him with a spear.
t.5.44.32: And the mighty Bhāsakarṇa, enraged, took up a spear, and the two of them stood together on one side, facing the illustrious tiger among monkeys.
t.5.44.34: His limbs wounded by those two, his body-hair smeared with blood, the enraged monkey became radiant like the rising sun.
t.5.44.35: Tearing off a mountain peak along with its beasts, serpents and trees, the heroic Hanumān, elephant among monkeys, struck down the two Rākṣasas.
t.5.44.36: Then, when those five generals had fallen, the monkey destroyed the remainder of that army.
t.5.44.37: With horses he destroyed horses, with elephants elephants, with warriors warriors, and with chariots chariots; that monkey laid them waste as the thousand-eyed Sahasrākṣa destroys the Asuras.
t.5.44.38: With slain elephants and horses, with great chariots whose axles were shattered, and with slain rākṣasas, the ground was blocked on every side, its paths obstructed.
t.5.44.39: Then the monkey, having slain in battle those heroic commanders of the army together with their forces and their mounts, the hero took up that same archway beam and stood biding his time, like Kāla at the destruction of all beings.
t.5.44.31: Then, knowing that those three had been slain by the mighty monkey, Praghasa, of great speed, forcefully rushed upon Hari.
